chunks: Via his chain to Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hisham ibn Salim from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said:

Abu Basir led us in prayer on the road to Mecca. He said while in prostration – and a camel of theirs had become lost: 'O Allah, return to so-and-so his camel.' Muhammad said: I entered to see Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him. He said: Did he do that? I said: Yes. He remained silent. I said: Should I repeat the prayer? He said: No.

key_terms.أَبُو بَصِيرٌ: Abu Basir, a companion of the Imams
key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.طَرِيقِ مَكَّةَ: The road to Mecca, indicating travel prayer context

ai.seo_question: Does making a specific supplication for a worldly matter during prostration require repeating the prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Tahdhib* highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding *sujud al-shukr* or general supplication during prayer, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) ruled that seeking a specific worldly need (a lost camel) does not break the prayer's validity. The initial silence of the Imam suggests a moment of consideration or confirmation of the act, but his final 'no' establishes that such specific, non-verbal or brief verbal requests do not constitute a nullifier (*mubtil*) of the prayer. This reflects the principle that minor, permissible actions or intentions within the prayer structure do not necessitate repetition, distinguishing it from major breaks like eating or speaking unnecessarily.
